transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith... my wife actually pushed me to make the appointment. She thinks I'm reading too much into things. I know she says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. And I get that workplaces can be chaotic. I mean, I'm a teaching assistant right now—working on my graduate degree—and the department is always sending

When your wife explains that these late meetings and message changes are just normal work stuff, does that reassurance ever settle your mind, or do you remain completely convinced something is going on regardless of what she says?

Well, I try to let it settle my mind. I really do want to believe her when she says it's just normal office stuff. But... for the past year, they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It's like there’s a private signal in those messages meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

Speaking of signals, it actually reminds me of this communications seminar I had to TA for last semester. The professor was completely obsessed with subtext and non-verbal cues. He made me grade these massive stacks of undergraduate papers, and honestly, the students these days just don't know how to format a basic bibliography. I spent three hours last Tuesday just correcting APA citations. It's exhausting, and the department doesn't even pay us enough for the extra hours we put in. I mean, they promised a stipend increase in the spring, but you know how university bureaucracy is. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my wife's work. Yeah, no, her telling me it's normal just doesn't explain the patterns I'm seeing.
Aside from your wife, do you find yourself generally suspicious or distrustful of other people in your life—like friends, coworkers, or family—or is this concern really centered only on her?

No, no, it's... it's really just her. I don't have any issues trusting my friends or my family or anything. Like, the other grad students in my cohort, we all get along perfectly fine. 

Take my friend Dave, for instance. He's a TA in the sociology department, and I'd trust him with my life. We actually co-hosted this midterm review session last weekend for the undergrads, and he brought these amazing homemade bran muffins. His wife bakes them. Apparently, she uses this substitute for butter—applesauce, I think? I didn't think it would work, but they were actually incredibly moist. I tried to get the recipe from him because I've been trying to watch my cholesterol lately. My primary care doctor told me at my last physical that my numbers were creeping up, which is honestly ridiculous because I barely eat red meat anymore. It’s mostly just chicken and rice these days, maybe some fish on Fridays if it's on sale at the local market. The prices of seafood have just gotten completely out of hand with inflation. 

But... sorry, what was I saying? Right, trusting people. Yeah, no, I don't have any problem with other people. Everyone else is fine. It's just... the things with my wife, they're just too specific to ignore.
Have you found yourself doing things like checking her phone or emails, tracking her whereabouts, or confronting her about these suspicions?

Well, I... I mean, I have confronted her, yes. We've had a lot of tense conversations at home about it. It's really putting a strain on the marriage. That's actually why we started seeing a couples therapist. The therapist was the one who suggested I come get an individual assessment, actually. She said it might be helpful. 

She's a nice lady, the therapist. Her office is in this old converted Victorian house downtown, right near that little coffee shop that sells those amazing almond croissants. I usually try to grab one before our sessions, but they sell out so fast. It's crazy, you have to get there before 9 AM or you're just out of luck. The barista there, a young kid, maybe a sophomore, was telling me they source their almonds from this specific farm in California. Apparently, the drought out there has been terrible for the almond yield. I read an article about it in the Times last week. It's fascinating how interconnected agriculture and climate are. I was thinking of incorporating some of that into my lesson plan for the intro seminar next week, just to give the undergrads a real-world example of systemic impact. 

But anyway, yeah, it's mostly just affected things at home with her. I haven't been missing work or anything. I still get up, shower, go to campus, grade papers... my usual routine is totally fine. It's just the marriage that's taking a hit.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a single, fixed, non-bizarre delusion of his wife's infidelity ('jealous type' delusional disorder), evidenced by his interpretation of ambiguous work-related behaviors (late meetings, message changes) as coded signals of infidelity, persisting for about a year despite reassurance and lack of corroborating evidence. There is no evidence of hallucinations, disorganized speech (aside from circumstantial tangents, which appear to reflect anxious over-inclusiveness rather than formal thought disorder), negative symptoms, or bizarre delusions. Functioning outside the marital domain remains intact (work, hygiene, social relationships with friends/colleagues are unaffected), and suspicion is circumscribed to his wife rather than pervasive/generalized distrust, which argues against paranoid personality disorder or schizophrenia. The encapsulated, non-bizarre, monothematic delusion with preserved functioning outside the delusional system is classic for Delusional Disorder, Jealous Type.
